content: Nursemaid's elbow, also known as radial head dislocation, is a condition where the radius bone in the elbow becomes dislocated. This means the bone slips out of its normal position at the elbow joint. When a child experiences nursemaid's elbow, they typically begin crying immediately due to pain in the elbow and refuse to use the affected arm. The child may hold the arm slightly bent at the elbow and pressed against their abdomen. While they may move their shoulder, they will avoid moving the elbow. Some children stop crying as the initial pain subsides but continue to avoid using the elbow. This condition is most commonly seen in children under the age of 5. It often occurs when a child is pulled too hard by the hand or wrist, such as when lifting them by one arm to help them over a curb or step. Other causes include breaking a fall with the arm, rolling over in an unusual way, or swinging a child by the arms during play. Once the elbow has dislocated, it is more likely to happen again, especially within the first 3 to 4 weeks after the initial injury. By the age of 5, a child’s joints and surrounding structures become stronger, making this injury less likely. However, in rare cases, it can occur in older children or adults, often due to a forearm fracture. Children under 5 years old are at the highest risk for nursemaid's elbow. A healthcare provider can diagnose nursemaid's elbow by examining the child. The child will typically be unable to rotate the arm at the elbow so that the palm faces upward and may have difficulty fully bending the elbow. If you suspect your child has a dislocated elbow or refuses to use an arm, you should seek medical care immediately. In some cases, the elbow may slip back into place on its own. However, it is still important for the child to be evaluated by a healthcare provider. Do not attempt to straighten or reposition the arm yourself, as this could cause further harm. You can apply an ice pack to the elbow and try to immobilize the area above and below the injury, including the shoulder and wrist, before taking the child to a doctor or emergency room. A healthcare provider will treat the dislocation by gently flexing the elbow and rotating the forearm so that the palm faces upward. This procedure should only be performed by a trained professional. If the condition recurs frequently, your healthcare provider may teach you how to correct the problem yourself. If nursemaid's elbow is left untreated, the child may permanently lose full range of motion in the elbow. With proper treatment, there is usually no permanent damage. In rare cases, complications may arise that limit the movement of the arm. To prevent nursemaid's elbow, avoid lifting a child by one arm, whether by the wrist or hand. Instead, lift the child from under the arms, by the upper arms, or by both arms. Do not swing children by the hands or forearms. If you wish to swing a child in circles, support them under the arms and keep their upper body close to yours.
